title: Hanuman carries them up
hook: the disguise comes off, and Hanuman carries two princes up the mountain

segments.voice: Yesterday: vakya, Hanuman's first words, and Rama's praise for them: true, kind, helpful speech is a practice. True, kind, helpful speech is a practice.
screen: `TRUE, KIND, HELPFUL SPEECH IS A PRACTICE.`

segments.voice: Now it's Lakshmana's turn to answer, and he does something you might not expect from a wary prince in a dangerous forest. He tells the stranger everything. Who they are. Why they're in exile. That Sita has been taken by a rakshasa while they were away, and they don't know where. That Kabandha sent them to find Sugriva. A wary prince might give a stranger the short version. Lakshmana gives the whole thing.
screen: `LAKSHMANA ANSWERS.` → `HE TELLS IT ALL.` → `NOT THE SHORT VERSION.`

segments.voice: Trust answered with trust. Hanuman spoke carefully and honestly, and Lakshmana meets that with the whole story, including a humbling sentence for a prince of Ayodhya: Rama, who used to be a refuge for others, has come to Sugriva for refuge. Hanuman is glad. Sugriva too has lost his wife and his kingdom, he says. You can help each other. Then the disguise comes off. He takes his own shape, a monkey, the son of the Wind. Rishyamuka is steep and the brothers have walked a long way, so he lifts them onto his shoulders and carries them up the mountain to Sugriva. Here's why that picture matters so much to Hindus. Hanuman is the great example of dasya, devotion as service: loving God by doing God's work, with no wish to be the hero. Hindu teachers count dasya among the classic ways of devotion, and Hanuman is the one they point to. So Hindus don't pray to Hanuman instead of Rama. They pray to him on the way to Rama. In many temples his image stands near Rama's, hands joined. Many families recite the Hanuman Chalisa, forty verses traditionally credited to the poet Tulsidas, often on Tuesdays and Saturdays, and one line calls him the guardian at Rama's door. Today's scene is that line in action: the servant who carries tired people to Rama. As for his name, the old bear Jambavan tells that story much later. As a baby he leapt at the rising sun, thinking it was a fruit, and Indra's thunderbolt struck his jaw, his hanu.
screen: `TRUST ANSWERED WITH TRUST.` · `CARRIED UP THE MOUNTAIN.` · then, large: `DASYA: LOVE THAT SERVES.` · `HANU: THE STRUCK JAW.`

segments.voice: Let your shoulders drop, and feel how much they carry on an ordinary day. If you pray, say the chant many Hindu families use, Shri Ram, jai Ram, jai jai Ram, softly on each out-breath, the way Hanuman keeps Rama's name. If you don't pray, breathe out slowly and bring to mind one person whose load you could help carry this week, without needing to be thanked.
Hanu, the jaw struck by Indra's thunderbolt, which gave Hanuman his name.
Your line: dasya, love that serves. Hanuman carries tired people to Rama and never asks to be the hero. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Images of Hanuman carrying Rama and Lakshmana on his shoulders are common in Hindu art. In many temples Hanuman's image stands near Rama's with hands joined, and many families recite the Hanuman Chalisa, often on Tuesdays and Saturdays.

Hanuman.meaning: son of the Wind, Sugriva's minister, devoted to Rama

Jambavan.meaning: the old bear who later tells Hanuman's birth story

Indra.meaning: king of the gods, whose thunderbolt struck baby Hanuman

Rishyamuka.meaning: the mountain where Sugriva hides from Vali

dasya.meaning: devotion as service, loving God by serving

Hanuman Chalisa.meaning: forty Hindi verses praising Hanuman, credited to Tulsidas
